rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient to reveal the full elution window while minimizing the risk of missing late compounds. This should show whether peaks are compressed early, spread across the gradient, or still retained into the high-organic hold.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the goal is to cut t_last below 10 min without sacrificing the weakest pair. Narrow the gradient to the observed elution window and shorten it to concentrate separation where the peaks actually elute.

We have the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be made faster while staying fully resolved. The current limiting pair is 6/7 at R=1.53, so reducing tG by one step is the cleanest test of the speed limit at fixed selectivity.

The 8 min gradient is too steep because pair 6/7 collapses, so keep tG at 10 min and raise temperature one step to try to shorten the run while preserving or possibly improving that selectivity-limited pair. This tests whether temperature can maintain full resolution with a bit less retention than the current optimum.

Higher temperature strongly hurt the critical 6/7 pair, so test one step lower than 40 C to see if cooler conditions increase that selectivity enough to create margin while still keeping t_last under 10 min. If so, we may gain a more robust optimum or create room for later time trimming elsewhere.

40 C is clearly the best temperature, so now keep the successful slope but narrow the upper end of the gradient slightly to better match the actual elution window and potentially improve the critical mid-run selectivity. This may retain enough speed while giving pair 6/7 a bit more room than the 0.65 endpoint.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical pair but made the run too long; now raise phi0 one step instead to trim early low-value gradient space while keeping the successful upper endpoint. This should test whether the same full resolution can be retained with a shorter overall retention window and possibly a better time-optimized maximum-CRF method.

Injection 7 improved both t_last and the critical 6/7 margin versus injection 2, so it is the best starting point for another speed test. Shortening tG by one step will show whether that added margin is enough to keep full resolution while reducing runtime further.

The best current method still has only a small margin on pair 6/7, and lowering phi1 previously strengthened that pair at the cost of retention. Combining the improved phi0=0.15 start with phi1=0.60 should test whether we can keep full resolution with a still-sub-10-minute last peak, potentially yielding a more robust optimum.

Raising phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 improved both speed and the limiting 6/7 pair, suggesting excess low-organic space is hurting efficiency. One more step to phi0=0.20 at the same endpoint and slope tests whether we can further trim dead gradient time while staying fully resolved and under 10 minutes.

The best fully resolved methods are around phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.65, with pair 6/7 as the clear limit; raising phi0 too far starts to erode that pair. Increasing phi1 one step from the robust phi0=0.15 condition may pull the last peak earlier while keeping enough selectivity to stay at full credit.

The fully resolved 10 min methods sit right on the edge for pair 6/7, while both higher phi1 and lower tG degrade it. A slightly longer gradient at the best window should strengthen the limiting pair and map the robustness boundary on the safe side of the current optimum.

The tradeoff is now clear: higher phi0 shortens the run but weakens 6/7, while lower phi1 strengthens 6/7 but lengthens the run. Combining both changes may balance those effects and could give a fully resolved method with t_last under 10 min and better margin than phi0=0.20, phi1=0.65.

Gradient and window changes have mapped a narrow optimum, and temperature clearly changes selectivity enough to switch which pair is limiting. A larger cooling step from the best window is worth testing once because it may improve the 6/7 pair enough to open room for faster conditions later, despite the risk of longer retention.

At 40 C the only question left is whether a different phi-window can also give full resolution with faster elution; prior results suggest lower phi0 helps the critical pair while higher phi1 shortens the tail. This combination directly tests that balance against the current two optimum methods.

The best methods are already found, but one remaining useful check is whether a modest cooling step from 40 C can preserve full resolution while offering a different robustness profile than the failed 25/35/45 C runs. This fills in the temperature map near the optimum without changing the proven gradient window.

Temperature is decisively optimized at 40 C, so the remaining unexplored local variable is the lower gradient start. Testing phi0=0.05 with the proven phi1 and tG will complete the phi0 map and confirm whether the optimum truly lies between 0.10 and 0.15.

The only plausible path to another full-resolution optimum is to trade a bit more upper-end strength for selectivity margin, but we need to see if that can be compensated by the favorable phi0=0.15 start. Testing phi1=0.55 completes the endpoint trend and checks whether the late peak still stays acceptably close to 10 minutes.

We have mapped the separate effects of raising phi0 and phi1, but not their combination at 40 C. This test checks whether a shorter, stronger window can still keep the critical pair near full credit while delivering the fastest fully observed run.

This completes the 40 C window map by pairing the lowest phi0 with the higher phi1, the one remaining unexplored corner near the current optimum region. It tests whether the extra low-end retention can preserve the critical 6/7 pair even with a stronger endpoint that may shorten the last peak.

A lower phi1 strongly improves the critical 6/7 pair, so combining that with the faster 8 min gradient is the best remaining chance to beat the failed 8 min methods and possibly recover full resolution at shorter runtime. This directly tests whether endpoint narrowing can offset the loss in resolution from the steeper slope.

The 8 min, phi1=0.60 test improved markedly over the 8 min, phi1=0.65 run, so the remaining question is whether the faster phi0=0.20 start can recover more time without collapsing resolution too far. This is the last informative 8 min corner near the best 40 C region.

With only three injections left and no way to exceed CRF 1.000, use the remaining budget to define the upper-end failure boundary around the successful 0.10/0.65/10/40 method. Raising phi1 another step should shorten the tail further and confirm how quickly the critical 6/7 pair degrades.

The last useful unexplored corner near the optimum is phi0=0.15 with the stronger phi1=0.75 endpoint. This will complete the local map around the two winning methods and confirm whether the phi0=0.15 window remains superior as phi1 is pushed higher.

For the final injection, probe one last untested boundary near the best region: higher phi0 with the more selective phi1=0.60 endpoint. This checks whether additional trimming of the low-organic segment can still maintain full resolution while offsetting the longer retention seen at lower phi1.
